subject: ent
title: Neck masses and neck dissection

steps.tx: The sternomastoid divides the neck into **anterior and posterior triangles**, further marked by the digastric, omohyoid and midline strap muscles. Age guides the differential diagnosis because children develop congenital and inflammatory lumps while young adults add lymphoma and salivary gland disease. In older adults a new neck lump is metastatic until proven otherwise. A left **supraclavicular node** often signals a primary below the clavicle, reaching the neck through the **thoracic duct**.
steps.say: The sternomastoid separates the neck into anterior and posterior triangles, with the digastric, omohyoid and strap muscles as further borders. Let age guide your differential because children develop congenital and inflammatory lumps while young adults add lymphoma and salivary disease. Doctors assess a new lump in an older adult as metastatic until biopsy proves otherwise. A left node above the collarbone often points to a primary below the clavicle, which drains upward through the thoracic duct.

steps.tx: Midline and lateral congenital cysts declare themselves by movement and site, and **thyroglossal duct cysts** rise with tongue protrusion and swallowing along the tract from the foramen caecum. The **Sistrunk operation** removes the cyst with the body of the hyoid and a core of tract tissue to prevent recurrence. **Branchial second cleft cysts** swell at the anterior border of the upper sternomastoid as fluctuant and transilluminant lumps, excised after infection settles. Brilliantly transilluminant multiloculated swelling in an infant suggests cystic hygroma, while a midline dermoid stays still on tongue protrusion.
steps.say: Suspect a thyroglossal duct cyst when a midline lump rises as the patient protrudes the tongue or swallows. Plan a Sistrunk operation that removes the cyst with the central hyoid and a core of tract tissue so recurrence stays unlikely. Suspect a second cleft cyst when a fluctuant and transilluminant swelling appears at the upper front edge of the sternomastoid, and excise it completely after infection settles. Regard a diffusely infiltrating and brilliantly transilluminant infant swelling as cystic hygroma, while a dermoid stays still on tongue movement.

vis.caption: Congenital neck cysts: thyroglossal duct (midline) and branchial cleft (lateral)

steps.tx: Workup of an adult neck mass starts with full examination of the upper aerodigestive tract covering the nasopharynx, tonsil, tongue base and larynx, followed by **fine needle aspiration** of the node with ultrasound guidance. Add **HPV and EBV testing** with thyroglobulin assay to narrow the primary site. The **unknown primary protocol** images the neck and chest, then examines the patient under anaesthesia with directed biopsies and tonsillectomy or tongue base mucosectomy in selected cases. Avoid open biopsy first because it seeds skin, distorts tissue planes and spoils later dissection.
steps.say: Doctors examine the whole upper aerodigestive tract first, including the nasopharynx, tonsil, tongue base and larynx, then sample the node with ultrasound guided fine needle aspiration. HPV and EBV studies with thyroglobulin assay help narrow the search for the primary tumour. Follow the unknown primary protocol with imaging of the neck and chest, followed by examination under anaesthesia with directed biopsies and tonsillectomy or tongue base surgery in selected cases. An early open biopsy remains forbidden because it seeds the skin and blocks later clean dissection.

steps.tx: Nodal **levels I to VII** map the dissection from the submental and submandibular basin through the jugular chain to the posterior triangle, central compartment and superior mediastinum. **Radical neck dissection** removes levels I to V with the sternomastoid, internal jugular vein and accessory nerve, while modified radical dissection preserves one or more of those structures. **Selective dissection** clears only the basins at risk, such as levels I to III for oral cavity cancer. Loss of the accessory nerve causes shoulder syndrome, and a milky left drain signals a chyle leak.
steps.say: Learners must know the nodal map from level I under the chin through the upper, middle and lower jugular chain to the posterior triangle and the central and mediastinal basins. Understand that radical dissection removes levels I to V with the sternomastoid, the internal jugular vein and the accessory nerve, while modified dissection keeps one or more of those structures. Choose selective dissection for the basins at risk, such as the upper three levels for oral cavity cancer. Surgeons protect the accessory nerve to keep shoulder movement, and a milky left drain indicates a chyle leak.

steps.tx: The illustration maps the nodal basins from **levels IA and IB** under the chin and jaw through levels II, III and IV along the jugular chain to level V in the posterior triangle. It also marks **level VI** in the central compartment and level VII in the superior mediastinum, with the sternomastoid, **internal jugular vein** and spinal accessory nerve shown beside the nodes. The inset contrasts selective, modified radical and radical dissection planes. Use this map in the exam to match each primary tumour with its expected basin.
steps.say: Study how the marked nodes run from under the chin and jaw down the jugular chain into the posterior triangle and the central and mediastinal basins. The panel keeps the sternomastoid, the blue internal jugular vein and the yellow spinal accessory nerve beside the nodal groups. Compare the inset panels that show which levels and structures selective, modified radical and radical dissection remove. Use this picture to link each primary tumour with its expected drainage basin during revision.
